text_translated_detailed: From Ternate, the 14th of June, Year 1751.— Register of Papers, as by order of the Esteemed and Honorable Gentlemen Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director together with the Council of these Moluccas, by the ship Rust en Werk [Rest and Work] from here via Macassar to Batavia were sent, consigned and described to His High Nobility, the High and Noble well-born greatly Honored Lord Jacob Mossel.— Governor General, together with the late Esteemed Gentlemen Councilors of the Netherlands Indies. BB: This Register.— No. 1: An original missive signed by the Governor and Council in Molucco, to the aforementioned Your High Nobility, of this date— No. 2: Copy of a report concerning the Cruise undertaken toward the Coast of Mindanao and the Karinganise Islands— No. 3.— A Copy of a resolution taken in the Council of Policy at Ternate of the date 27th of August of the year past.— No. 4: Two pieces of drafts on the Ternate Trade books 487 of the year 1749, and 17 7/50.— No. 5:—. Reports of the Confrontation made on the same. From Ternate, the 12th of June, Year 1751.— No. 6: A Case with described Trade papers of the same years 17 7/49 and 17 25/50.— No. 7:— Same, same described Salary Papers of the year 17 7/50.— No. 8: The Collections or positive orders drawn from the successive [orders] through Your High Nobility to Ternate and the remaining Eastern Government and separated letters since the year 1739 to 1749, inclusive.— No. 9: An Original Signed Report from the under-Merchant and Small Cashier Jan Hendrik Borwater, and the bookkeeper and First-sworn Clerk of Policy Bastiaan Ruijbroeck concerning the Seizure of Gold Cloth made.— No. 10: Bill of Lading and invoice of the cargo loaded in the bringer hereof.— No. 11: Arrival record of this vessel Ternate in the Castle Orange on the 12th of June, Year 1751 [was signed] I.s Thornton, secretary.

text_translated_detailed: Communication of the receipt of Your High Nobility's honored missive and enclosures. From Ternate, the 14th of June, Year 1751: Batavia. By the Ship Rust en Werk [Rest and Work] via Macassar. text_translated_detailed: In July 1751, a convention was taken and a decision made at our session of May 12th of that year. Having taken into deliberation the re-establishment of this gold-yielding post, whose rivers would otherwise be sought out by all manner of Bugis pirates, and the Honored Company would be deprived of those costly ores, and having further noted that this post previously stood so far inland that the Buginese not only were able to freely navigate the river, but could also obstruct the exit of it from our settlements, we resolved on that same day to order the resident Scherens to proceed in person to Lemboen [Lemboken], and to carefully inspect whether the aforementioned post could not be placed closer to the river in such a way that they could dispute the Bugis pirates' entry into it, and could defend the village against a hostile attack, with orders to provide us with the necessary clarification regarding his findings, whether by way of Manado [Manado] or directly. Furthermore, we resolved to garrison this post again with one sergeant, two corporals, and twelve common soldiers. The aforementioned gentleman, the Chialoup [uncertain: vessel type] De Cruijsser, in the midst of Xulla [uncertain: location], having arrived here at the roadstead on the 20th of June of that year, brought from there from Gorontalo two elderly female slaves and two small children of the murdered sergeant at Lemboken of Ternate. On the 20th of July in the year 1751, two elderly female slaves and two small children, then belonging to the kitchen of the massacred Sergeant Maaten Pietersz, who had absconded from the Buginese rabble during the recapture of the aforementioned post Lembonen, and were handed over by the commander of the aforementioned Chialoup, Dirk van Ameijden, as well as two sailors and one boatswain, whom the aforementioned pilot and the commander of the Pantjallang de Cacakoe, Jan Daemes, apprehended together.

Arrival of Major Friscus van Pijanda. Upon request of the chief military honors such as those of Macassar. From Ternate on the 20th of July 1751. Furthermore, we shall also note that Major Christoffel Friscus, having arrived here from Banda on the 13th of this month, was not only granted a seat in our council meeting of the 16th in the political council, but was also entrusted with the command as head of the military here, which shall also be divided into three Companies forthwith; and we must moreover humbly report to your High Excellency and Great Esteemed [title], that the Chief Merchant and Second Jeronimus Tonneman [to whom the chief administration was handed over by the Merchant and Fiscal Jacob Fredrik Stegman under the last of April in the year with an even balance] at our sitting of the 6th of this month made it known that a Chief Merchant at Macassar at the Castle's merchant Tonneman, in order to show military honor, was given the musket on shoulder and an officer for the front, whereas here he receives no more than the musket at the foot and a sergeant comes to the front, with the request that the aforementioned honor, such as is in use at Macassar, might be granted here as well, which we have accorded to the said Chief Merchant Tonneman for reasons cited in the said resolution, and we take the liberty hereby to humbly beseech your High Excellency and Great Esteemed [title] to furnish us in the coming year with a general regulation regarding how the military honors shall be given to the qualified persons here

Concerning the Colleges, and first of all that of the Council of Policy, we shall note that the Council of Policy, in accordance with what was established in our resolution of the 11th of January of the year, the prescribed Oath of purge was duly performed by us in proper form, and moreover in the formulas of the respective Oaths, both in this College as in all others, the name and titles of His Serene Highness the Prince of Orange and Nassau &c &c &c have been inserted, such as the order sent to us by your High Excellencies dictates, and furthermore on the 16th of April, 3rd and 24th of May of the year, the Captain Military Jan Hendrik Holmer, who arrived here this year from Batavia, the Chief Merchant Jeronimus Tonneman, as well as the Sub-merchant Jacob Coek Ceffie, who arrived from Gorontalo, were granted seats in this council, while furthermore with regard to the College of Justice we shall set down that we, according to our decisions of the 23rd of December of the past year and the 29th of January of this year, upon the proposal made by the president of that court, the aforementioned chief administrator Jacob Fredrik Stegman, have appointed to the same the Military Flag-bearer Endgh Christiaan Wiggers and the Chief Surgeon of this Castle Adam Boone, and furthermore on the 16th of April following thereupon, also as guardians. Thereupon the under-merchant Johannes Pauwen [Iohannes Pauwen] being ordered to step outside the meeting hall, and the same having been complied with, it became apparent to this council not without great displeasure that these commissioners, Pauwen and de Jager, contrary to the orders given to them, visited only a part of the south-east corner of Mindanao [magindanauw], and did not at all steer toward the islands of Jolo [Xullok] and Paguanma [Pagunma], and moreover during their said commission could not obtain any more merchandise for the Company than 45 pounds of wax in exchange for so much iron, and 18 pounds of caret or tortoiseshell for a piece of blue flag cloth. But since they at the end of their said report come to state that there is on the island of Mindanao [magindanauw] and the islands lying around it absolutely no trade to be done for the Company from Ternate [Ternaten] under date 20th July 1751, it has been unanimously deemed good and resolved to send the said report to their High Excellencies at Batavia [Batavia] and to request their High Excellencies' much wiser judgment and decision in this matter, and to await their much-esteemed orders as to whether, based on the assurance given by the commissioners, this expedition shall be discontinued or whether another trial shall be made of it. Subsequently, for such reasons as are mentioned in the said report, the appointment by the ship's officers of the Constable of the yacht the Gertrude [Geertruijda], Jacob Baemer [Iacob baemer] of Stralsund [Straal sond], as second mate has been approved, and at the same time his wages have been increased from 20 guilders [ƒ 20:] to 24 guilders [ƒ24:—] per month in order that his current contract, which shall expire on the 19th [of the month].

text_translated_detailed: ship the Geertruijda, Huijbert van der Kneu, the pro-tem second mate Jacob Breemer, the boatswain Lourens Lont, the sailor Andries de Ruijter, and the sailmaker Thobias van Harlingen, all likewise stationed on the aforementioned vessel, who, in favor of the upright truth and at the request of the skipper of the aforementioned yacht Stephanus de Jager, declared how true and truthful it is that on the 8th of July in the year lying here at the roadstead ready to sail, at noon twelve o'clock the house anchor having been weighed in the morning, the daily rope broke, and thereby the aforementioned rope with the anchor was lost, without that the same, notwithstanding all efforts applied, could be recovered again, just as the attestants also declare that when then by inspection of the second rope seven fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 42 meters] were cut from the same and obtained for ship's service, it was damaged, since the Company's vessel could not be trusted for that. Furthermore the attestants also declare how true and truthful it is that on the 8th of August following, through heavy weather and rough seas, the yacht pitched so heavily that a three-pounder cannon placed on the bow was struck out of the rampart and cast into the sea, and likewise a large sail, a bazan [uncertain: type of sail], and a lee sail were torn almost half to shreds, completely torn to pieces, so that the same were irreparable, for which reason the scraps were used both for repairs and other ship's services, all of which the aforementioned declaring attestants declare to be the pure truth, whereupon, being prepared to confirm the same with a solemn oath. From Ternate under date 20 July in the year 1751. text_translated_detailed: The Company's valuable spices certainly deserved to be undertaken, with the following proposition: since the yacht the Geertruijda lies at the roadstead without any employment, this visit could conveniently be carried out with the same vessel. However, it was necessary first to weigh the advice of our equipment master Jan Jonkers, whom His Excellency had appointed for this purpose before the assembly hall, and this pilot was subsequently summoned. After the aforementioned matter had been discussed with him, he declared that the said cruise could be undertaken with no greater expectation of good success than could now be achieved, and that it could most easily be accomplished by the end of February or mid-March next. Regarding this, Van Ternaten, under date of July 20th, 1751, deliberated further, and all necessary considerations having been taken into account, it was unanimously resolved and decided that the cruise should proceed following the examples of the years 1726 and 1728, beginning from the north side, and that the yacht the Geertruijda should be projected for this expedition. Since we currently have no other capable servants available for this purpose, this commission is to be demanded from the skipper of that vessel, Stephanus de Jager, and the other ship's officers, and furthermore that keel is still to be reinforced with the remaining sailors who were on the wrecked bark the Susanna Catharina and are expected daily from Xullabessij. Since from our garrison, of which one hundred soldiers are here, more than thirty men lie sick in the hospital, no manpower can be spared. Furthermore, the aforementioned officers are to be provided with an appropriate and proper instruction for their guidance. Moreover, the expended gunpowder by the officers of the yacht the Geertruijda from the fifteenth of June to the fifteenth of October last has been passed for write-off, as the now summarized and inserted below gunpowder account dictates. text_translated_detailed: and Andries de Ruijter, boatswain and sailor of the yacht the Geertruijda lying here at the roadstead, taking the liberty in the name and on behalf of the assembled crew of the aforementioned vessel, humbly to represent that they, in the first week of the month of February of this year, sailed from Batavia hither, and subsequently were dispatched to Mindanao and Saringan for the purpose of cruising, and upon their arrival here, to their sorrowful distress they discovered that through the failure to send their accounts to the Schulte [uncertain: "rlecq:"] here they had to continue without payment. Without that they, in all that time, received more than one month of their wages (which were earned through sweat and labor), whereby they have fallen into the highest degree of poverty, and are no longer able to protect their naked bodies from the heat of the day, rain, cold, and other hardships. Therefore the supplicants, as well as all the sailors, in all humility turning themselves to your Esteemed Honors, most humbly request that, since each one has a good sum to their credit in wages, the supplicants together with the remaining sailors may be strengthened with three months' pay to each, for as much as each one's wages amount to, so that they may relieve themselves in their impoverished and needy state and may again provide themselves with covering for their bodies. From Ternate under date 20 July 1751. From Ternate under date 20 July 1751. — As it pleased your Esteemed Honors, the undersigned in the month of March last was ordered with the Pantjallang the Clara to proceed to conduct a cruise along the north coast of Celebes and for that purpose was furnished with a written Instruction whereby the same was ordered to serve your Esteemed Honors upon return with a report in writing: in observance of which the undersigned now has the honor to do so hereby, and first to set forth that with the aforementioned small vessel dated the 27th of the last passed month of April, the Manadose roadstead being reached, where, in the performance of various matters, we remained until the 21st of May thereafter, from where subsequently to further the assigned Commission we departed and on the 24th of the month of June arrived at the roadstead of Tontoli, where on the 5th of the following month of July there arrived a Buolereese prau with the under-master of that post through whom we were informed that at the village of Clanckagaal where the Tontoli's Goegoegoe was residing (and not far from our anchorage place) two Thodong vessels had arrived, upon which news everything was made ready to send the boat to the aforementioned vessels, since the vessel drew too much water to be able to come to that place, and it was possible to overcome them, which they did that night at 12 o'clock together with the aforementioned Buolereese prau which had four soldiers from that post, together with an islander named Intje Malaijoe (who had himself spoken with the Thodongs) on board, all well provided with ammunition and weapons, but upon arrival there we learned that they had that same evening already departed from there

Today the 27th of October 1750, there appeared before me Thomas Thornton, [expanded: pro loco] secretary of this Government, in the presence of the aforementioned witnesses — the quartermaster Thomas van der Sanden, and the sailors Hermanus van Wijk and Jacobus van der Post, all residing on the Pantchiallang de Clara now lying at the roadstead here, who all three together, and each of them individually, in favor of the truth and at the request of their master, the under-steersman Jacobus Wijdemans, declare to be true and truthful that they with their aforementioned vessel departed from here on the 24th of March of that year, and being driven by contrary wind and current, on the 1st of April thereafter, were forced to come to anchor with a drag in the bay of Telolo, and subsequently on the 7th thereof, when wanting to wind the drag to continue their journey to Manado, the drag rope came to break at the hawsehole, whereby the aforementioned rope iron with 50 to 55 fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 90-100 meters] of hemp rope, without the fault of anyone, was lost, and notwithstanding all efforts applied, they were unable to recover the same. — With which the attestants concluded their declaration, giving as reasons for knowledge as already set forth in the text, being ready to confirm the same if necessary with a solemn oath. — Thus done and attested at Ternate Orange on the aforementioned date in the presence of Pieter van Dam and Johan Gebrecht Seidelman, both clerks as

Friday the 27th of November in the year 1750, and Your Esteemed and Honorable Mister Governor and Director of the Moluccas [Moluccos] in the morning meeting present — Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Esteemed as chief merchant and second — Jacob Fredrik Stegman, as under-merchant and garrison bookkeeper — Matthijs van Peenen, and from Ternate under date 20th July in the year 1751 — the under-merchant — Jan Hendrik Bouwater, deputy as such and provisional official — Johannes Pauwen, by indisposition. At the beginning of this meeting the Governor produced a letter from the under-merchant and Manado resident Gerrard de Goede dated the 5th of this month, by whose summary it being seen that through the great drought the rivers in the Bwool gold mines are without water, and the workers, gravediggers, are therefore unable to deliver the gold they have dug, because they cannot wash and purify the same from their earth and filth, yet that after the fall of rain, a good yield of that precious mineral was expected, and also that the resident, at the request of the Bwool King and his nobles, has taken the Captain there called Bagunda to Manado in good security, and will send him with the first ship opportunity together with the documents in his charge hither, since the aforesaid little prince and his nobles, according to a Malay missive written to the resident and now sent hither, have come to lodge a series of complaints against him Bagunder, as the same is seen in the translation made here and inserted below. text_translated_detailed: Translation of a Malay letter written and sent by the King of Buol and his nobles to the resident at Manado. — Manado - To the highly esteemed and honored Lord Resident of our Gerard the Good. Under-merchant and resident of ours, who holds the power and governance over us collectively. — Honored Lord. — By this means I, King Jacobus Pompa, together with the gogugu [chief/noble] Manuel Tamataun and the Captain Laut Jacob Bale, as well as the hocum [chief official] Joseph Bille, make known on behalf of Captain Bagunda and his children, who have been establishing the Muhammadan faith here in our village of Buol, and there is also another person from Mindanao, called Pakel, who is in the house of the aforementioned Captain, and he is their priest. Furthermore, in the month of Powas [Islamic month], the aforementioned Captain, as well as Pakel and his son called Poeloe, have called all Christians to enter into the Muhammadan faith. And at the time when they opened the Powas [celebration], Captain Bagunda together with Pakel and his son again called all Christians together to perform their service behind the village from evening until eight o'clock in the morning, and this applied to both men and women. Upon this, the King sent a soldier with the Sergeant Commander to go together with the schoolmaster to inspect, so that we would not afterwards be called liars, just as the Commandant also sent a soldier named Mattheos Lotokan together with the schoolmaster Dominicus Jansz, who went together to inspect these matters. And then the aforementioned master and soldier found this to be true, not just once but several times, as often as the Powas occurred. For this reason, I, King Jacob Pompa, and gogugu of Ternate, dated

text_translated_detailed: Jacob Cobb: of the following content. To the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director, together with the Council in Molucco. Esteemed and Honorable Lord and Gentlemen.— In accordance with Your Esteemed and Honorable always much revered order, the undersigned, having been expressly commissioned thereto, proceeded to Ternate under date 20 July 1755.— As Chief Merchant and Head Administrator Jacob Frederik Stegman, and there the specifications of the Office Culla during the Command of the late Sergeant Jan Jacob Cobb, until the 7th of September of this year, have been exactly compared against the principal account books, and therein found such errors as are here below specifically to be demonstrated, namely regarding shortage. We find ourselves obliged to elucidate for the reasons given alongside, that the confronters, as noted by the late Commander Cobb, in the last year of his Command has been qualified, so that such a Commandant all 6 months not more than one hundred rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch currency] to slaves as laborers on the barque for the payment of food provisions to the occupied Susanna Catharina in service 118: 27½ rixdollars in cash, that such provisions were indeed necessary to take without it being approved for payment and resolved the remainder thereof, cash monies were sent there, over which the same according to a specification from their High Excellencies from the Company's Treasury to the heirs of the said Commander Cobb from his own purse have been paid, and whereby then also this majority causes to be reimbursed.— by the books to be entered. 452.—: Item.

Having thus far obtained possession of the aforementioned matters, the Governor reminds the Council of the King of Ternate. Under date 20 July 1755. Tidore, regarding the Council's very emphatic letter of 14 February, which was received by Malay dispatch of the 14th of the month [uncertain: "rabularer"] 1163. With respect to those still wandering about Maba and elsewhere, having served in response that these people (with the exception of one or two who still held their residence in the forest) had all been sent back to their former positions, and His Majesty, by rescription of the 15th of April following thereafter, was placed before in a very forceful and serious manner, how His Majesty, according to the explicit content of Article 7 of the concluded peace treaty, had been obliged to have these mountain dwellers returned to their villages but to be handed over to the Esteemed Company, in order that they might be delivered to their lawful sovereign, the King of Ternate, and this Council would continue to await the effect thereof. However, the King of Tidore not only let the same pass unnoticed but also since that time has made the least mention of it in his letters, as the aforementioned matter stood. But His Excellency, having meanwhile understood that these alphoreses would truly be returned to their former positions, had ordered his interpreter and translator Matthijs Daenet to inquire by all occasions (yet in a concealed manner) whether the aforementioned current rumors were true or not. This interpreter, a few days ago, had provided a written report, which he subsequently produced and was found to contain: To the Esteemed and Honorable Mister Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director of these Moluccas. Esteemed and Honorable Sir. It having pleased Your Esteemed Excellency to order the undersigned

It having pleased Your Esteemed Excellency to order the undersigned to inquire by all occasions whether the Ternatan alphoreses, who in the recent war between the courts of Ternate and Tidore had fled from their positions to Maba, Waijssili, and elsewhere under the rule of the latter sovereign, committing many robberies and murders, and who are still wandering about, have returned: so the undersigned has the honor hereby to inform Your Esteemed Excellency in the form of a report that, in accordance with the aforementioned high order of the King of Ternate under date 20 July 1751, he has let no occasion pass by to obtain information about how matters stood with these wandering mountain dwellers, without having been able to succeed until a few days ago, when the reporter came to the dwelling house of the Macassan Hoen, being a person who daily frequents the village and among the great ones of Ternate. Thus then by these means Your Honors' son and King, together with his assembled bodatosses, makes known to his father, the Honorable and esteemed Lord Governor and the assembled council, concerning the power of the Alfurese Alfurese people, which at present weighs heavily upon Tidore, together with many deaths, which have begun in the month of Cawal Islamic month, and until now have not ceased, so that His Majesty and his bodatosses make this known to Your Honors, Esteemed Lord Governor and council, begging that this shall cause no displeasure, for to whom else shall we make this known but to the Honorable Company, and likewise on the village where Your Honors' son and King resides, people die daily, and sometimes as many as eight persons, and at the least that die is five or six men, so that he is greatly grieved by the multitude of people who die there, and even more because we have no burial cloth, therefore Your Honors' son and King is requesting of Your Honors, Esteemed Lord and Father, together with the assembled council, to be helpful to us, for fifty pieces of Cloves, twenty pieces of fine parcels, ten

E. v. Mijlendonk, J. C. Stegman, J. H. Tborwater. — of the Moluccas. From Ternate dated 20 July 1750. Monday the 11th of January 1751, in the forenoon. Meeting present: the Honorable and esteemed Lord Governor and Director Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, the Honorable Chief Merchant and Second, Jacob Fredrik Stegman, Under-Dispenser and Garrison Bookkeeper, Matthijs van Peenen, and Jan Hendrik Borwater, Deputy, the same, Principal Fiscal, Johannes Pauwen, absent due to indisposition. The Governor having proposed to the Members that the time had come to take, according to the permanent order of their High Honors, the established yearly Oath of Burgher, subsequently asks whether each one of them is ready and prepared for this, which was answered with Yes by each and every one, whereupon first His Honor and subsequently the members each in particular, after the reading of the form prepared for this purpose and sent from Batavia, without any exception, took the aforementioned oath in due form, after which the following finding was resumed: Finding of such goods as were given in the month of August in the year 1748 to the captain of the Susanna Catharina, Jan Stuijt, going on a cruise along the coast of Halmahera and Saringanij, and until now by the aforementioned have not been accounted for or answered for regarding shortage on the voyage, which has been lost, and [illegible] — 3. — pieces of Bethille Ternate cloth held by the undersigned — 10. Carekams, blue red sourats [uncertain: type of cloth]. /understood:/ Ternate in Castle Orange, the 18th.

text_translated_detailed: Under-merchant, Dispenser and Garrison Bookkeeper, Matthijs van Peenen, Jan Hendrik Borwater, Deputy, and Small Cashier, and P.L. Fiscal, Johannes Pauw, and by disposition. First, the liberation was taken regarding the vacancy of Small Cashier and Hospital, due to the death of the Surgeon Jan de Hiesen, by whom these offices had been held, which first position of Small Cashier was subsequently demanded and assigned upon the approval of Her High Excellencies, and having made a request in this regard, Under-merchant Jan Hendrik Borwater was urged, with the admonition to him that he would be required to provide sureties in the Company's matter, and since from the servants available here, for the hospital position no one other than the Surgeon of this Castle, Adam Boone, has come to request it, he was likewise appointed to the hospital position upon the approval of the aforementioned Her High Excellencies, in the expectation that he will provide the suffering sick with the best of the necessary food suitable for their illness. Hereafter the Governor gives the members to understand how, since His Excellency's presence here, he has observed that the frequent sending of commissioners to the court of Ternate, in order to urge and admonish the prince to the fulfillment of such points as he promised in the combined meeting of the 5th of April 1718 to carry out, tends more to the detriment of the Company's interests in that respect than to the advancement of matters, since upon the sending of commissioners from His Highness, the first two members of this meeting from Ternate, under date 20 July 1750, are always employed, the prince being found each time alone and without any council member accompanying him, who then upon the presentation of their commission would indeed give a sufficient answer and assurance.

Your Esteemed Lordships and Gentlemen, Johanna van Roon, widow and housekeeper of her deceased husband, the late Caspier Willem Geel, takes the liberty with all humility and lowliness to present to Your Esteemed Lordships that the aforementioned her husband, together with and alongside the subordinate and Gorontalo resident Jacob Scherens, was generally constituted by the junior merchant then Manado resident Jacob [unclear] in [unclear] and was appointed, and now as fiscal [expanded: financial officer] Johannes Pauwen, together with the position of the supplicant's husband in the year 1748. Upon his coming to pass away, the administration was taken over by the general junior merchant Scherens. Furthermore, upon the arrival of the aforementioned junior merchant Pauwen from Manado here, he demanded accounts from both the supplicants and from the general Scherens. To do which the supplicant, out of ignorance and inability, was compelled to rely on the promise of the aforementioned Scherens that before his departure to Gorontalo, he would settle the matters with the here Pauwen, so that the supplicant would receive no further demands in the future. The supplicant left the matters to him all the more because he was also executor of the supplicant's deceased husband's testament, which was subsequently demanded and demanded from the supplicant by the aforementioned with Pauwen in the month of June of that year, and a desk [a piece of furniture] where the papers of her deceased husband were kept, under the pretext that they were needed for the settling of accounts. This desk was also handed over by the supplicant, out of simplicity and out of good trust in the aforementioned gentlemen Pauwen and Scherens, because the first was the supplicant's husband's full sister and the last was her husband's executor's friend. Yet, giving trust out of the heart, this trust has come to stand against the supplicant, for after the departure of the junior merchant Scherens to Gorontalo, not knowing better whether the matters were fully, at least sufficiently settled, yet

text_translated_detailed: General Cashier Willem Geel, Johanna van Roon, had made her complaint to Your Excellencies in writing most bitterly regarding the injustice and violence done to her by order of the undersigned, in that by his wife and slaves all her goods were forcibly removed from her dwelling house and brought to mine, wherefore Your Excellencies by the aforesaid setting had deemed it good to immediately after the division and the same two members together with the secretary to send to my dwelling with order and instruction to tell me and to order that, standing ready as the goods were removed by the wife of the aforementioned widow from the dwelling house of the aforesaid widow in a violent manner in the presence of the aforesaid members, to restore them and after proper inventory to have all of them brought back by my own people to where they came from. Upon which I made known to the aforesaid members that there were no goods of theirs removed from their dwelling house by order of me or anyone of mine by force, but rather that they, on account of a certain debt owed to me (now more than a month ago) at their own request and with their knowledge had handed over goods to my wife, and on this account the appointed commissioners at their request, in order to inform Your Excellencies before they proceeded with their assigned task, but they gave in answer that they had no order for this, but rather that the matter, as aforesaid, should immediately proceed as before, as also happened, concerning all of which Your Excellencies have further deigned to order the undersigned to, within the time of three days after receipt of the aforesaid extract, submit in writing the reasons and motives which have caused me to undertake this improper and against all rights contrary treatment, upon which I have the honor then to say in the last

text_translated_detailed: But rather that the matter, as aforesaid, should immediately proceed as before, as also happened, concerning all of which Your Excellencies have further deigned to order the undersigned to, within the time of three days after receipt of the aforesaid extract, submit in writing the reasons and motives which have caused me to undertake this improper and against all rights contrary treatment, upon which I have the honor then to say in the last instance: I have never thought of such a thing, and much less perpetrated it regarding the aforementioned widow, but rather, as mentioned before, briefly as cited above, regarding a certain debt owed to me, on her own offer and request, she handed over some goods (which also was more than a month before we were here) for the P. [Prosecutor] to have sold, except for those which her husband had shortened from me, in order to take those back for the principal, which I have also done or agreed to, so that I cannot sufficiently wonder and be amazed how the widow could have come to Your Excellencies with such false and practiced lies, and since the undersigned and his wife find themselves greatly injured and offended by this, my most humble request is that proper satisfaction may be given to me by the aforementioned widow on this account. I could have added many other matters here to further strengthen this my innocence, had my bodily condition permitted it, which is why I then have the honor to name myself with deep respect. Understood: Your Excellencies, gentlemen and sirs. Lower: Your Excellencies' obedient and humble servant. Was signed: Johannes Pauwen. In margin: Perwaten, orange [uncertain: possibly a date designation], 23 January 1751. To the Esteemed and Excellent Gentlemen: the Governor and Director of the Moluccas, Jan Bliss van Mylendonk, E. [Esteemed] P. [Prosecutor] S. [Senior] Chief Merchant & standing. From Ternate under date 20 July 1751.

text_translated_detailed: Johannes Pauwen, as fiscal [legal officer], was charged with this matter, and the Council of Justice was ordered to have him answer for his violent words. At the same time, the undersigned Jan Hendrik Borwater was appointed as officer for this purpose, in order to prosecute the aforementioned fiscal Pauwen before the aforementioned Council of Justice, and there to promote the rights of the high authority, as well as those of the widow Geel, as shall be deemed necessary according to law, with further decree, in order to have Borwater provided with an extract of this document and below the copies of the submitted complaint through the aforementioned widow Geel, the report inserted here before, with the answer of the aforementioned fiscal Pauwen, on the aforementioned extract resolution of the 19th of this month, so that he may be able to serve accordingly. Considering this matter, given that the aforementioned fiscal Pauwen, through the intermittent course of now better and then worse, has been dragging on for about seven weeks, the affairs of Justice are coming to be greatly neglected, and principally because the commanding officer of the wrecked ship Pallabessij, the Susanna Catharina, Jan Stuijt and the master of the ship's carpenters Phemer Jansz. Roseboom and two helmsmen from the keel Hans Matthijsz and Jan Shurbrood, which according to resolution of the 31st of July of the past year are placed in the fiscal's custody without payment of maintenance costs or wages up to this date, continuing without process having been instituted for this up to now, notwithstanding that they have already been in Cullabissij here since the month of November of the past year, whereby these people must fall into great poverty, it is therefore also resolved and decided to have the papers pertaining to the aforementioned process from the fiscal Pauwen be demanded, and to have them placed in the hands of the said sub-merchant Borwater, with express order to proceed as quickly as possible with these procedures before the Council of Justice

text_translated_detailed: Tomadjiko. Simathaoe. Malajoeknohra. Malajoe T Chim. Tafaga. Tobamnoetoe & ditto. Lobeleuw, ditto. According to the agreement of yesterday, the king of Ternate through the principal merchant and chief administrator Jacob Fredrik Stegman and the sub-merchant and dispenser Mathis van Peenen, was fetched from his palace and approached the Castle, and at the guardroom of the officer on watch, was received by the governor with the customary ceremony, welcomed and conducted to the upper hall of His Excellency. Being there, His Highness was subsequently placed on the balcony, where the prince, having refreshed himself for about half an hour, His Excellency then enters with the prince, the councilors and His Highness's royal councilors in the ordered council chamber, where each being seated, the Governor reminded the king that His Highness at a combined meeting of the 5th of April in the year 1749, when His Excellency's predecessor was still here in good standing, certain matters were presented to him which, although His Highness had promised to fulfill them, yet to this day remain in the same state as they were at that time, notwithstanding that His Highness has been reminded of this several times, both through official channels and otherwise, and since Her High Excellencies have already been notified of this and the time is approaching when this council will have to report again to Her High Excellencies how far and to what extent progress has been made with these outstanding matters, the Governor therefore reminded the king that His Highness, together with his royal nobles, had requested this meeting for this purpose to present these matters again to the prince, and indeed initially on the 8th of the month of [uncertain: abbreviation] of the year 1748, the senghadja of Gammaknorra, Jdaija called, was appointed together with the shopkeeper, who held the authority during the minority of that chief

text_translated_detailed: is the Manado resident to write to the kings and great lords of Buol in serious manner, yet nonetheless in a friendly way, that those of Tontoli have already brought their new fortifications to completion, whereby they are now protected and defended against the attack of all foreign pirates, whereas they on the contrary have been sufficiently encouraged to also jointly set hands to work and to build their new fortification with speed, so that it may likewise serve them as a retreat and place of resistance for all those who might come to attempt any harmful undertaking. Subsequently the resident notes that the king and great lords of Tontoli have requested another sergeant and commandant in place of the Jan Semransz [uncertain: possibly a name] posted there, and this on the grounds that he has only one eye, and they do not wish to have a commandant who has any bodily defects, with which reason the Corporal Claas Wenwersteed [uncertain: possibly a name], who had been previously proposed by them, was taken into consideration. Item, it being further taken into account that the resident in his aforementioned letter maintains that it is indeed necessary to place a sergeant at Tontoli, one who is a soldier, the keeper with the native and sergeant at Tontoli to be stationed, the first soldier knows how to deal with it, since those native peoples alone require particular guidance, without however setting aside that these qualities are found in the aforementioned Corporal, for which reason on this matter it has been resolved and decided to authorize the resident to place the aforementioned Corporal Wenwersteed, who is endowed with the aforesaid qualities, as commandant at Tontoli, and to have Sergeant Simonsz return to Manado by ship with orders that we must be informed of this with all speed, so that we may be able to grant our approval thereafter. Considering all of this with attention and taking into account that the disturbances arising from the aforementioned Tobieders and Tobaards, if they are not checked and opposed at the beginning, can produce nothing other than an undoubted rupture in these Moluccas, especially since these settlement peoples have conducted themselves in the recent war in no other way than through murder and plunder, and their bloodthirsty dispositions having been aroused through these hostilities, and moreover the strongest party of these warring mountain people having been forced to withdraw to the fortress, it is certain that they will return to those places from which they have only recently returned, and will then think only of means to give free rein to their insatiable murderous and plundering lust. text_translated_detailed: letter from the sergeant and commandant at Dodingo, Balthazar Gosman, the content of which, insofar as it is relevant to this matter, follows as follows. Ternate. To the Esteemed and Honorable Mister Jan Elias van Mylendonk, Governor and Director of these Moluccas. Esteemed, Honorable, Valiant, Esteemed and Very Generous Sir. After a humble and courteous salutation to Your Esteemed Honors, it serves only to make known to His Esteemed Honors that the round timbers taken from the forest have been retrieved, except for four, of which nearly half I have been able to fish out of the sea, which I assure His Esteemed Honors, and I will request a vessel to first retrieve half of those round timbers. Furthermore, I make known to His Esteemed Honors that the Senghadje of Cauw with his Bebetas have requested that I make known that a Moor from the settlement of Cauw by the name of Penua, who has sold a free Alfurese to the Mabarese, which the Mabarese has killed, and moreover has sold six Alfurese as slaves, and that the Senghadja with his Bobatas request that this Moor be brought to land. [Understood] Your Esteemed Honors' most humble, obedient and obedient servant [was signed] Barth: Gosman [in the margin:] Dodingo, to be understood the 19th of February 1750. Regarding all of this, it has also been resolved to have the prince understand, with the consequences that are to be expected from this, namely a total collapse of his realm and subjects, since the footsteps of the aforementioned His Majesty's sister are being followed by all profit-seeking and grasping settlement heads and princes, and if this is not prevented in time, it will be followed, and thereby the settlements will be emptied of people and His Majesty's subjects will be forced to abandon their dwellings and go elsewhere, to escape the grasping hands of their settlement

confirmed until approximately mid-November of the past year, namely those which, due to the indisposition of the aforementioned Cashier, were denied by the then secretary of this Council, Thomas Chornton, until mid-January of the current year, have been drawn up, both against the issued ordinances as well as the ledger books of this government, and by which the first-mentioned shortage was found to amount to rixdollars [modern equivalent: Dutch colonial currency] 202.47.8, and by the last-mentioned rixdollars 6.44.8, or together rixdollars 209.44, as can be seen more clearly from the report attached hereto below.

To the Esteemed and Honorable Mister Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Directors of these Moluccas.

Esteemed and Honorable Commanding Sir,

In accordance with your Esteemed Honors' esteemed written ordinance of the 3rd of February of the current year, we, the undersigned, have proceeded to the accounting office and there, in the presence of the principal chief merchant and head administrator Jacob Fredrik Stegman, have carefully examined the respective cash specifications drawn up by the deceased small Cashier Jan de Niesen from mid-January 1749 until approximately mid-November 1750, as well as those which, due to the indisposition of the aforementioned small Cashier de Niesen, were drawn up by the Esteemed Secretary of Police Thomas Thornsson from mid-January of that year, both against the ordinances as well as the ledger books of this government, and have found them to be in exact agreement, and furthermore discovered that upon the examination of the aforementioned cash, a shortage of rixdollars 202.47.8 was found by the first, and in the administration of the accounts rixdollars 44.8, thus together rixdollars 209.44. With this we hope to have satisfied your Esteemed Honors' intention, as we take the liberty to name ourselves, with all humility and respect, your Esteemed Honors' most obedient and dutiful servants.

Signed: P.R. Pirker, J.D. Velde

In the margin: Ternate, dated the 19th of February

text_translated_detailed: Somarang, who on the 21st of July of the past year were apprehended in the Bwool gold mines, as officer to examine, I now have the honor to report to your Esteemed Honors that I have examined the aforementioned three persons, first each individually and then jointly, and questioned them as to why they had ventured beyond their territory into the aforementioned Bwool gold mines, which they then declared unanimously and as if from one mouth, according to the attached collected confession, that they, with their sixteen persons, were sent by a certain Prince named D'ain Manampa, who resides on Paquano, in order to visit his brother named Marsolij Ponoa, who was then lying ill on Bwool, and on the way, at a certain place called Lekuk Bogouw, having crossed the river with the three of them in order to seek a prau [a type of boat] with which they could continue their journey further to Bwool, they then encountered the Bwool Captain Bagunda, who brought them to the gold mines, to the Bwool Captain named Lauz Baloe, who subsequently brought them to Bwool and handed them over for safekeeping, and they also subsequently received no further news from their abandoned companions or comrades, this then, Esteemed and Honorable Sir and Gentlemen, is what was declared by the aforementioned three persons, which also fully agrees with what was written by the Manado resident Egerrard de Goede, without, however, it being established or appearing from the confession given by the aforementioned persons that they had engaged in the aforementioned gold mines with any malicious intent. For this reason the undersigned, under correction and with deference to your Esteemed Honors' better judgment, must testify that I cannot pursue any further legal action against these people, but maintain that they, paying nothing for the costs, should be released from custody and could be sent back to their place of residence at the first available opportunity. On the 13th of February, Anno 1750, there appeared before the undersigned members of the Esteemed Honorable Council of Justice of this Castle, together with me, the secretary, the Limbotters named Doemarie, Pong Alo, and Somarang, the first and last from Tomillo and the third from Lembotten, who, each individually, being heard and questioned by the undersigned and fiscal in this matter, Jan Hendrik Borwater, confessed unanimously, in the manner as follows: that they, with their companions, were sent by a certain Prince named Kit Chiel D'ain Manampa, residing on Paquano, in order to visit his brother named Marsolij Ponoa, who was residing on Bwool and was ill, and coming to a certain place called Schuk Bojau, from there they crossed the river with the three of them in order to seek a prau, so that they could travel to Bwool, leaving their companions at the aforementioned place, and then they encountered the Bwool Captain Bagunda, who brought them to the gold mines together with the Bwool Captain named Laawt Baloe, the headman, who handed them over for safekeeping, without the confessants having heard further from their companions, with the addition that they are not slaves but free-born subjects. text_translated_detailed: The sergeant of His Excellency's guard, the corps of Matthijs Grijs, was continuously ordered to arrange, in accordance with His Highness's instructions to our commissioners, dated the 24th of February, to send commissioners to Tobillo and Tobaro, with the purpose of suppressing the disturbances that had arisen between the peoples of those two villages and removing them from the way. Thus the governor said that His Excellency, in accordance with that decision, after the aforementioned meeting had been adjourned, had summoned the cited sergeant and charged him with the task of urging the prince to send commissioners to the aforementioned villages of Tobillo and Tobaro. This Crijger reported the following afternoon that the king had promised to send his commissioners as quickly as possible. However, from Van Ternate [Ternate], dated the 25th of July 1750, until today, nothing whatsoever had come of it. Rather, His Highness, on one day and then another, gave nothing but contradictory, nonsensical, and variable answers to His Excellency's further pressing, as is abundantly evident from the Moluccan daily register kept on the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, and 5th of this month. Nevertheless, His Highness, on the 8th of this month, in response to His Excellency's unceasing exhortations, replied that the sending of commissioners was not now necessary, since a good number of both principal and lesser subjects from Tabillo and Tobaro had already arrived here, and that His Highness had sent his sergeant, called Hassan, to the aforementioned villages to summon the remaining principal and lesser subjects to come here as well, and that the prince, when they have also arrived here, would not only remove the disturbances that had arisen and establish peace among them, but would also appoint another senghadje [chief administrator] over the toll collectors in place of the murdered one.

Excellencies, my Lords, and Gentlemen, according to the instruction also given to us dated the 29th of September of the past year, we weighed anchor on the 20th thereof and directed our course according to the content of the sailing orders handed to us, and likewise pursued our voyage around the great spice island Halmahera and the islands lying thereabouts in such manner as was clearly and distinctly prescribed to us by the said instruction. To avoid all prolixity which would only cause Your Excellencies displeasure, we shall not in this matter make a repetition of the places, islands, harbors, and inlets where we have anchored, cruised, and investigated, nor what happened to us at each place, since this, if it please you, can be seen from our kept journal or daily notes. But we shall, under hope in expectation of favorable tidings, have the honor to set down in general that we have visited and inspected all islands and places set down in our instruction and sailing orders with all carefulness, as much as was possible to us. To the Honorable, Esteemed, Venerable Lord Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director together with the Council in the Moluccas, Honorable, Esteemed, Venerable commanding Lord and Lords, Stephanus de Jager, captain, Huijbert van der Kineu, chief steersman, Andries de Ruijter, boatswain, Jan Jansz van der Beek, sailor, and Joachim Voerman, Constable, all stationed on the ship the Geertruijda, which is now lying at Talingawij for repairs, take by these means the liberty on behalf and in the name of all the sailors of the aforementioned vessel to make known to Your Honorable Excellencies that they, in the month of November of the year past, notwithstanding that they were all in debt according to the account, have through Your Honorable Excellencies' great favor been benefited with a provision of three months' wages for as much as each one's wages amounted to, and since that time they have made a voyage around the coast of Halmahera without that since that time any voyage or their return has yet yielded them any earned wages for nine months, wherefore the supplicants as well as all the sailors are turning themselves to Your Honorable Excellencies humbly requesting that it may please Your Honorable Excellencies, out of consideration for the great poverty in which they find themselves, graciously to allow each of the supplicants as well as all their subordinate sailors five months' wages to be provided, so that they may provide themselves with some necessary bodily sustenance. From Ternate, dated 20 July 1751 —

Therefore, with a unanimous vote, it has been decided to send that keel back to Batavia. Moreover, at this opportunity, of Ternate under date of 20 July 1750, having taken into mature deliberation and consideration the meager supply of rice here and the fact that there is not a single vessel on hand to be able to have that grain fetched from Manado. Item, furthermore, it having been noted that in the Tomini Bay cruising vessels, the Yacht the Compliance and the Bark Buuren, after their expedition, if they were found suitable for this, could in this time of the blowing southeast-southwest monsoon very easily cross from Gorontalo to Manado in order to take on a cargo of that grain, it has been deemed good and decided to order the Gorontalo resident to inquire, upon the return of the aforementioned vessels from the Tomini Bay, of the authorities there whether they consider their keels to be in a condition to be able to fetch a cargo of rice from Manado. Item, should they come to declare themselves capable of this, the aforementioned resident is to be ordered to dispatch them there as quickly as possible, not further than the resident De Goede to Manado. Extract.

The Military Captain Ian hendrik Solmer makes known to the governor that the most recent military personnel who arrived here with the ships the Galathea and Rustenwerk from Batavia, as well as various others who have been in garrison here for a long time, are completely destitute of uniforms, and in general cannot be outfitted as soldiers, since through their poverty they are unable to procure the same themselves, with urgent request for the necessary goods to be provided, as is done in the other eastern provinces, from the great trading warehouse at thirty percent advance. In order that each soldier in need may be provided with a uniform consisting of a coat and breeches, it was deliberated and approved and resolved to grant the captain's request and to issue to him as much linen cloth at thirty percent advance as shall be necessary for making new uniforms, but the forty-nine pieces of hats at fifty percent advance are to be paid for, with further order that the responsibility for the making of said clothes be assigned to the aforementioned Captain Holmer. But I leave what is mentioned here to his Excellency's much wise judgment. Undertaken. Hereby I remain his Excellency's always obligated servant. Was signed. Jan Sochem bunger. All of this having been approved and understood, it was decided to allow payment here, with no further decision being made to the supplicants regarding the following request, as well as to provide the assembled sailors of the aforementioned vessel rest and work, granting three months' wages instead of the requested four months, as appears from their petition submitted from Ternate under the date of the 20th of July 1751.

To the Honorable and Esteemed Mister Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director, together with the Council in Molucco.

Honorable and Esteemed Sirs and Gentlemen,

Cornelis Pietersz. Ribbe, boatswain, and Jurgen Sits, constable, described as being on the ship Christen [uncertain: possibly "Christen" or similar name] lying here at the roadstead, do hereby take the liberty, in the name and on behalf of the assembled sailors of the said vessel, to make known to your Honors that they departed from the chief place of the Indies in the month of February in the year of our Lord [J.D.] without their wage accounts having been sent along here, and since the supplicants as well as the other sailors find themselves completely deprived of bodily sustenance and clothing, they take it upon themselves, in the name aforesaid, to turn to your Honors with humble request that it may please your Honors, out of consideration for the needy state in which they find themselves, to graciously grant to each of the supplicants, together with all their subordinate sailors, four months' wages, so that they may obtain some relief from their present difficulties. It is hoped that this will be granted, in the name of the assembled sailors of the said ship Rust en Werk [Rest and Work], and was signed by Cornelis Pietersz. Ribbe and Jurriaan Fritsz. In the margin: Ternate, Orange [the month], the 24th of May in the year 1751. Further noted by Lager: the needy state of the supplicants herein is known to me, and was signed.

text_translated_detailed: The Commandant said he could defend a thousand men, especially since the King of Pargie has promised to erect a new fortification for the settlements. — Noble and Esteemed Gentlemen, we cannot refrain, before departing from this matter, from expressing to your Noble Esteemed Selves that all cruising expeditions conducted by large ships, or vessels, indeed even by small boats [Chialopen: small rowing vessels] in this bay are entirely in vain, and serve only to incur heavy expenses for the Esteemed Company, inasmuch as these same vessels are always in danger of shipwreck due to the reefs and rocks that lie along the shores of this bay, and can do the enemy no harm whatsoever; moreover, in the case of a landing, little can be accomplished, because one encounters nothing but marshes and dense forests. However, according to our humble opinion, it would be of greater advantage to the Esteemed Company, with less cost and less trouble, if year after year two well-armed raiding vessels [stroopant Chiallangs: raiding boats] were to come cruising at the mouth of the bay, which could hide themselves just as the pirates do behind the islands that lie in the bay, and could surprise and seize the vessels with which they enter the bay in such a manner, and thus their trade, which they conduct, would be shut down. For it is otherwise impossible to frighten away these pirates so that they do not come into the bay and plunder and rob whatever they can seize. From Ternate, dated 20 July 1751. text_translated_detailed: Express thereto nominated commissioners the Flag-bearers Moroten Weggers from his Dwelling was fetched Some matters had before Van Ternate under Date 20 July 1751 carried and was thereupon by his E: E: Produced A sworn Declaration regarding the loss of Two p:s [pieces] Anchors One Grapnel And Fifteen Fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 27 meters] Cable-rope by the Authorities of the Bark Buuren on the Journey to Gorontalo Reading Today the 3rd June Appeared before me Thomas Thounton Secretary of this Government present the aforementioned Witnesses the Under-steersman John Frederik dubordien Boatswain Ari Jansz: and Dirk Eggers Sailmaker all in Company's service and stationed at the then repair wharf on Salingama Lying bark Buuren which they acknowledged and Declare to the truth of the matter and at the Requisition of their Commander the Upper Steersman Jurriaan Pietersz: Gaaij that on the 12th August Anno past Sailing toward Gorontalo at night with the going out of the First watch a drought We perceived C East the potter in two-water to be which syl: strongly approached immediately the rudder was brought to Lay Deeds to turn away from it that failed and thus having run aground Brought two Anchors out and remained there lying until the day when under the anchor Winding the Cable-rope 10 to 12 Fathoms [modern equivalent: approximately 18-22 meters] from the anchor came to break Just as also under the Lowering of the second Anchor the grapnel rope shortly by the anchor was Broken whereby aforementioned rope Van Ternate Under Date 20 July 1751 Iron and Fifteen fathoms rope without doing or negligence of Anyone lost have because the buoys by the strong currents Underwater reached having after all applied efforts in vain no possibility was There to get said anchors back again as by Inspection of the aforementioned Grapnel-rope the same found unfit: In order our bottom

The first mate Jur Van Ternaten, under date 20 July 1751, Juriaan Pietersz Gaaij, having given a declaration anew for recollection, having been presented thereby and still remaining unchanged, persisting without desiring that anything be added to or taken from it, then subsequently took the oath in proper form under the raising of the two foremost fingers of their right hand and the uttering of the following words: "So truly help me God Almighty" [understood]. Done and sworn at Ternate, Orange, under the aforementioned date [was signed]: Johan Fredrik du Bordieu, Arij Jansz, and Dirk Eggers [lower:] quod attestor [was signed]: E.C.n Weggers and Clement Marct. And since it has thereby become apparent that the unavoidable loss of the aforementioned goods was for the preservation of that keel, so it was deemed good and understood to have the one and the other written into the business books, likewise also in order to the sailors of the aforementioned bark, instead of the requested five months' wages, according to the following request of the petitioner, on the debt account, no more than three months' wages shall be provided.

To the Noble and Esteemed Lord Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director, together with the Council in the Moluccas, Noble and Esteemed Lord and Gentlemen: Giving with due respect and reverence to know, Johan Frederik du Bordieu, first mate, Arij Jansz, boatswain, and Dirk Eggers, sailor, all described on the bark of Ternate lying here at the roadstead, under date 20 July 1751, Buuren, how they in the month of June of the past year were projected from here to Gorontalo, but the voyage could not be made in the month of August due to contrary wind and current, and they came here again to the roadstead, and on the 8th of that month began and completed for the second time, without having enjoyed more than two months' wages to Gorontalo during that time, whereby the petitioners, as well as all the sailors of those vessels, have been brought to the utmost state of poverty and see no chance of being able to rescue themselves from it unless Your Esteemed Lordship would be pleased to grant the petitioners and all the sailors some wages, as they take the liberty on behalf of themselves as well as for their shipmates who are on board in this hope to beseech Your Lordship that they, from the nine months which they have earned during their voyage with the Honored Company with so much danger, trouble, and hardship, may be granted five months' wages to each person, for which benevolence the petitioners shall here express their gratitude [understood]: the which request [was signed]: Johan F.k du Bordeau, Arij Jansz, and Dirk Eggers [in margin:] Ternate, Orange, 7 June 1751. text_translated_detailed: under the date of the 20th of July in the year 1751, Council of the Moluccas, Esteemed and Honorable Mister and Gentlemen. In order to serve Your Esteemed and Honorable in the shortest and most concise manner with the requested report concerning the matter of Wossie and its destruction, with the circumstances thereof, insofar as the one and the other could be ascertained from the accompanying documents, I shall be obliged to serve, for greater understanding and comprehension of the various residents, with regard to the extraordinary necessity that has befallen them, that the undersigned first sets forth a historical account, both concerning the situation and condition of this region, and also and principally what changes the same has undergone regarding the latter, since it has repeatedly done so over several years. It should first be known that in the Strait of Patience [Patani Strait] there lay five villages with the names Gaane, Saketta, Massja, Toija, and Wossie, of which the first was always directly under the rule of the Ternate king, and the others under the subordinate authority of the Singhalje [chief] of Cajoâ, which Singhalje, owing to lack of people and power, could not maintain himself on the island bearing his name and now uninhabited, when the Tidorese made their usual incursions and piracies, for which reason he had to decide to go over to Macquam with his remaining men there, where the Macquam chiefs granted him and a piece of land, and he established a village there, and has since been a participant in all the misfortunes that befell Macquam, no more and no less than one of the other chiefs, having made his interests common with theirs. Thus, when the Macquamers resolved to withdraw from the unbearable and intolerable arrogance of the Ternate court in the year [uncertain: text appears damaged], and with that purpose sought refuge with the Tidore king, they surrendered themselves to him, and likewise the Singhalje of Cajoâ also followed, but apparently more out of necessity than of their own free will, since three of the aforementioned villages in the Strait of Patience, namely Massa, Toija, and Wossie, had already previously, against his will and without his consent, gone over to the Singhalje of Weda, who was under the Tidore king. It cannot have escaped Your Esteemed and Honorable that with much effort and labor on the Company's part, in order to calm this Macquam affair, and to restore the inhabitants of that island under the obedience of their legitimate ruler, all proved fruitless, so that one was then forced, in order not to allow the power of Tidore to increase with the weakening of Ternate, to take those islanders, who were ready to undergo anything, as it were, to undergo the Ternate rule again, first under the immediate temporary rule of the Esteemed Company, awaiting a suitable opportunity to bring them to recognition of Ternate authority, and thus the aforementioned Singhalje of Cajoâ was then also placed under the Esteemed Company, among the number of those whom the Tidore king, after the conclusion of the peace and in the time of the Mister Governor Lelivelt, surrendered to the Esteemed Company, nevertheless, since in the peace contract

text_translated_detailed: of the Honorable Company to take, awaiting a suitable opportunity to bring the same to the recognition of the Ternate authority, and thus it is that at that time Caioa was already more commonly reckoned among the Honorable Company, being among the number of those whom the King of Tidore after the conclusion of peace and during the time of the Lord Governor Lelivelt handed over to the Honorable Company. Nevertheless, the Macquanders and the Senghaji of Caioa were received under the temporal administration of the Honorable Company. His Highness of Ternate, however, regarding all adverse occurrences concerning that island, was to provide communication. Thus this matter at that time found its settlement, to the satisfaction of both rulers, until there followed upon it the destruction of the village.

text_translated_detailed: to wish one another with the aforementioned Supreme Governor General new or first-time luck and blessing under Ternate under date 20 July 1751, with the bestowal of all desirable blessings upon the most highly esteemed his Illustrious Highnesses the highly esteemed house of Orange, the Governor then with both the Kings proceeded thereafter to the balcony from where one saw on the plain of this Castle in good order arrayed the military garrison, the pensioners and burgher company, the companies of the Macassars, Ternates, and Doreans, all under their officers and with Orange cockades on their hats and sashes, and as the Governor had commanded the aforementioned company to silence and attention, they were given the aforementioned documents, and also through the secretary read aloud, and thereupon asked whether they would hold the oath of loyalty to the most highly esteemed his Highness as their Supreme Governor General and honor and respect his Highness in that Eminent Character, which by them with a general expression of joy of "yes" and three-fold cries of "Orange" was confirmed, whereupon all aforementioned companies each in turn fired three volleys from their hand weapons, between each volley interspersed with a cannon shot from the wall, and thereafter all the heavy cannon of Castle Orange, the Point Voorburg, and the ships lying in the roadstead, the Galathea and Geertruyda, and likewise the smaller vessels from above to below with flags and pennants shortened were fired, and thus that very joyful day was concluded with a well-arranged banquet, which in honor of this ceremony was given at the Company's expense, and that memorable day was spent with all signs of perfect contentment. Thus ended it [uncertain: onderstond]. Thus done and established at Ternate in Castle Orange, dated as aforesaid, was signed: Jan Elias van Meylendonk, Jeronimus

text_translated_detailed: 1751 Council of Policy at Ternate [Ternaten] On the 21st of October 1750 and 15th of March 1751 Made and Delivered to the Esteemed and Honorable Mister Jan Elias van Mylendonk, Governor and Director together with the Council in the Moluccas, by the Under-Merchant and former Gorontalo President Jacob Coek. The aforementioned report being of the following content: To the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Jan Elias van Mijlendonk, Governor and Director, together with the Council of the Moluccas, Esteemed and Honorable Lord and Gentlemen. The undersigned, in accordance with Your Esteemed Honors' much-esteemed order, having examined three prisoners brought here by the shallop the Cruiser from the bay of Taminij, hereby wishes to inform Your Esteemed Honors that two of them, by name Moenij and Pongodeul, are peloppers, a nation that, as has long been known, in the aforementioned bay as well as on the west coast of Celebes, wander with no other purpose than to dig for gold or trade and carry such to their land, to the great detriment of the Company's trade. Which the aforementioned two peloppers also were, according to their own confession, this annex containing that they, with their king named Pamea, came to Parigi, and there and in the surrounding bay, by digging for gold, made their profit as was their custom, adding further to their excuse that they did not know that such a prohibition from the Esteemed Company was in place from Ternate, under date 20 July 1750, which however is not admissible, since so many expeditions have been undertaken by the Company in that direction for the establishment of the Company's private gold trade and the prevention of all smuggling in that precious commodity. It cannot be unknown to anyone there that the Esteemed Company alone has the right, to the exclusion of all others, to trade there. The third prisoner is a personal slave of the Boetons Captain Lieutenant Lauwtlandigen, who also allowed himself to be found in the plundering of the Post Lemboene, but afterward having fled, wandered for some time on the bay until he was captured at Paigie and handed over to the Esteemed Company. From the aforementioned, it shall be clear to Your Esteemed Honors that the three prisoners in this matter are at best unauthorized wanderers and smugglers of the Company's trade, as well as enemies of its allies, all of which conduct the well-known order of the Esteemed Company dictates shall be put in chains and sent to Batavia in order to work there on the common works, which punishment the undersigned also [under correction:] submits that the three aforementioned prisoners may be rightfully applied to. text_translated_detailed: His Highness said to me at the outset that he had understood that the three sitting in detention here—Timorese Maja, Captain, and Manicke—with the ships standing ready for their departure would be sent in chains to Batavia, and asked me at the same time whether such was indeed proper. I answered the Prince that I could not give him an answer without special orders from Your Excellency's Honor. Upon this he continued that the King, that he would very much like to see that the second-named, or Captain, might be excused from this, since the sister of the same was one of the concubines of His Highness, for whom His Highness held very great affection, which His Highness had fallen to his feet and in a submissive manner had requested, if it were possible, to work toward it that the aforesaid, her brother Captain, would not be sent, or that she could not obtain such from a tender longing and love for the same; his departure from here would not be well endured by her, but she would bring herself to an end. Under date of 20 July 1751 at Ternate, this request, accompanied by a multitude of tears, had so affected His Highness that yesterday (as this matter then took place) he could not refrain from shedding tears, with tears rolling down his cheeks again in the course of this discourse, full of hope. I answered that I could do nothing more in this matter than to present what His Highness had said to Your Excellency's Honor, and wished to take my leave, when the Prince said to me to request of Your Excellency's Honor in his name a favorable consideration of what has been set forth above, and to be willing to grant the same. With which I have the honor to serve Your Excellency's Honor with this account (understood) Well

To his High Lordship the High and Noble, Most Honorable Lord Jacob Mossel, Governor-General, together with the well-born Noble Lords Councillors of the Dutch Indies. High and Noble, most honorable, gentlemen, wise, prudent, discreet, and most generous Lord and Lords—. By our humble letters of the 20th of July in the year past /: as per the departing following description ship the Galathea original, as well as with the Yacht the Gertrude in duplicate dispatched :/ we have had the honor to render you, High and Noble, Most Honorable, a dutiful report of what until that time and the surroundings of these Moluccas had occurred and was carried out by us; we find ourselves now newly obliged to bring before your High and Noble Lordship by these means that which since that time, in the service of the Esteemed Company here has passed, and been accomplished by us, wherein we shall observe brevity as much as possible, and following that your High and Noble Lordship Most Honorable shall be informed in advance that the King of Chiauw Daniel Jacobs on the 23rd of August last arrived here, which potentate we shall now also be well maintained over. Report from the Manado resident "the rice and the extension of the post! for the neighboring reasons concludes to place on Kema 1 Corps and such dates. From Ternate on the 15th of September 1751. text_translated_detailed: Zalihiel alias Lemdhidin, Bilahihel Manansah, king who reigns on the land of Tidon with his assembled bobatassem [uncertain: likely a title or rank] their many affectionate greetings are sending to their esteemed friends the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Ian Elias van Mijlendonk Governor and Director of these Moluccas begging that the Almighty will be pleased to grant his peace and thus forever in this world besides a long life and good health for all time amen. So I am hereby making known to the Esteemed and Honorable Lord Governor and assembled Council regarding the doings of Anocada Tabaliku whose goods on Aebaina have been taken away, and because his Majesty and the nobles of the realm knowing nowhere better to address themselves to obtain compensation for the aforementioned goods than to their good and well-disposed friends who from Ternate dated the 15th are also merciful forever so that according to our thoughts we with true sincerity have also made the same known to their High Excellencies at Batavia and thus by consideration of his High Excellency and further Council of India having been approved to assist us in such matters according to good and well-disposed friends entirely, so that we are now setting forth the quantity of the Goods namely 28 Papuan slaves each at Reals 30: 35½ picul [modern equivalent: approximately 2 kg] of Massoy 10. paradise birds at each 30 stuivers [modern equivalent: Dutch currency]: per piece 3: chests per piece 7: reals 3: silver bowls weighing each in value per piece reals 6. 3. bolts of silk fabric with gold stripes in value - „ 10 1 . text_translated_detailed: [having observed] that the numerous embassies sent to the King of Ternate [to persuade the prince to fill the positions of Ternate that have been vacant for already five years—namely those of Goegoegoe, Captain Lauwt, and Stoetum—have repeatedly been fruitless. Therefore, following the embassy sent in the month of June, that work had begun to be set in motion, which had resulted in the sergeant of the Company's Bodyguard reporting this morning in the name of the prince that His Majesty intended to send his Great Men of the Realm to this Castle toward evening, in order to present to this Council a person whom His Majesty had chosen to fill the position of Goegoegoe. However, since the aforementioned sergeant did not know how to say who the person was whom the prince would have put forward for that dignity, His Excellency had ordered him to ascertain by all means and methods who it was. Subsequently he had been able to report that it was the present quimelaha [title] Marsaolij Patty Rana, as he is called, whom the prince would have put forward. When this matter and consideration were taken into account, two following points were examined: First, that the aforementioned Pattij Rana is a son of the Goegoegoe Marsaolij, who in the year 1719 was put to death by this same King for various bad practices and the embezzlement of the Company's spices. However, neither in the papers of the years 1719 and 1720 nor in the remaining Memoir of the Well-Esteemed, Great and Venerable Lord Commissioner of these Moluccas, Cornelis Hasselaar, was it found that the aforementioned pattij Rana or his family was excluded from the office of goegoegoe on account of the crime of his father, especially since he has already for a long time performed the office of quimelaha Marsaolij to the satisfaction of the court of Ternate
